snippet.description:
For decades, Lenny Strollo quietly ruled the criminal underworld of Youngstown, Ohio — running one of the largest illegal gambling operations in American history, corrupting public officials, and ordering violent hits to protect his empire.

This is the true story of how a low-profile businessman became the most powerful Mafia boss in the Mahoning Valley… and how his own decisions ultimately brought down an entire criminal network.

Inside this video, you’ll learn:
-How Strollo ran a multi-million-dollar illegal casino in plain sight
-Why Youngstown earned the nickname “Crimetown, USA”
-The shocking Christmas Eve assassination attempt on a prosecutor
-How mob money infiltrated law enforcement and local politics
-Why Strollo became one of the highest-ranking mob bosses to ever cooperate with the FBI

How his testimony helped trigger dozens of convictions and collapse a Mafia stronghold

This isn’t a New York or Chicago Mafia story — it’s about how organized crime thrived in a forgotten industrial city, and how loyalty, fear, and corruption eventually turned inward.

If you’re interested in true crime, Mafia history, political corruption, or FBI investigations, this story exposes how deep the system really went.

snippet.title: Real Russell Bufalino: The Quiet Don Behind 'The Irishman' Was the Most Dangerous
snippet.description:
He sold curtains in a dying coal town. He never raised his voice. He sat in a wheelchair in a federal prison medical center and still decided who lived and who died in cities he had never visited. This is the story of Russell Bufalino, the Quiet Don of Pennsylvania, the most powerful and least understood mafia boss of the 20th century.

In this deep-dive documentary, you will learn:
• How a 2-year-old Sicilian immigrant rose to control the entire garment industry of Northeastern Pennsylvania
 • The full inside story of the 1957 Apalachin Meeting — the catastrophic mob summit Bufalino personally organized, which exposed the existence of the Mafia to J. Edgar Hoover and the world
 • How Russell sat as a quiet adviser to the National Commission, mediating disputes between bosses like Carlo Gambino, Vito Genovese, and Tommy Lucchese
 • His alleged CIA recruitment in the 1960 plot to assassinate Fidel Castro before the Bay of Pigs invasion
 • The truth behind Frank “The Irishman” Sheeran’s deathbed confession and Bufalino’s alleged role in the July 30, 1975 disappearance of Jimmy Hoffa from the Machus Red Fox restaurant parking lot
 • The 1977 extortion conviction and 1981 murder conspiracy conviction that finally put him behind bars at age 78
 • How he continued running his empire from a wheelchair at the U.S. Medical Center for Federal Prisoners in Springfield, Missouri
 • Why his acting boss Billy D’Elia eventually flipped and confirmed everything the FBI had suspected for 60 years

Key figures: 
Russell Bufalino, Frank “The Irishman” Sheeran, Jimmy Hoffa, Joseph Barbara, Stefano Magaddino, Vito Genovese, Carlo Gambino, Sergeant Edgar D. Croswell, Billy D’Elia, Albert Anastasia, Joe Pesci (portrayed Bufalino in Martin Scorsese’s “The Irishman,” 2019).

Timeline: 
1903 birth in Sicily → 1953 FBI identification as top Pittston mob figure → November 14, 1957 Apalachin Meeting raid → 1959 ascension to boss → 1960-61 alleged CIA Castro plot → July 30, 1975 Hoffa disappearance → 1977 extortion conviction → 1981 murder conspiracy conviction → February 25, 1994 death at age 90.

Why this story matters today: 
Bufalino’s model of silent, relationship-based criminal power influenced every modern criminal enterprise from white-collar fraud rings to international cartels. The patient, low-profile boss is now the dominant archetype of organized crime in the 21st century — and Russell Bufalino wrote the playbook.

Sources include: 
FBI files, the Pennsylvania Organized Crime Commission 1980 report, Charles Brandt’s “I Heard You Paint Houses” (2004), and contemporary reporting from the Times Leader and Wikipedia archives.

snippet.title: The Real Zé Pequeno Was the Most Dangerous Gangster Behind 'City of God' Movie
snippet.description:
Before 'City Of God' became one of the greatest crime films ever made, it was a muddy housing project on the edge of Rio, built in 1966 to hide the city’s poor after a catastrophic flood. Within 15 years, it had become the deadliest neighborhood in one of the deadliest cities on earth. This is how it happened.

In this deep dive you’ll learn:
 • How Governor Carlos Lacerda’s “removalism” policy created the favela in 1966
 • Why the military dictatorship accidentally invented the Comando Vermelho on Ilha Grande prison island
 • How the 1980 cocaine boom transformed petty crime into industrial warfare
 • The true rise of José Eduardo Barreto Conceição — “Dadinho” / Zé Pequeno
 • The tragic real story of Manoel Machado Rocha, the man called Knockout Ned
 • How researcher Alba Zaluar and her assistant Paulo Lins documented the war
 • Why the 2002 film both helped and stigmatized 40,000 real residents
 • What Cidade de Deus looks like today under the militias

Key figures: 
Paulo Lins (author, born 1958), José Eduardo Barreto Conceição “Zé Pequeno” (1957-1985), Manoel Machado Rocha “Mané Galinha” (1952-1979), Carlos Lacerda (governor), Alba Zaluar (anthropologist), Fernando Meirelles (director).

Timeline: 
1966 flood and forced relocation → 1970s rise of petty crime → late 1970s arrival of the Comando Vermelho → 1979 outbreak of the Pequeno-Galinha war → 1985 death of Zé Pequeno → 1997 publication of Paulo Lins’ novel → 2002 release of the film → 2009 UPP pacification → present-day militia control.

Why it matters: 
Cidade de Deus is not a historical artifact. It is a living case study in what happens when a state decides poor citizens don’t deserve infrastructure, schools, or police protection. The same patterns are repeating today across Latin America.

 • Roberto Schwarz, “City of God,” New Left Review — https://newleftreview.org/issues/ii12/articles/roberto-schwarz-city-of-god.pdf
 • The Guardian, “Postcard from Hell” (2006) — https://www.theguardian.com/books/2006/jul/15/featuresreviews.guardianreview17

snippet.title: From Debtor’s Prison to the American Civil War | S1E1 | A House Through Time
snippet.description:
In the first episode of this series David Olusoga follows the stories of the first inhabitants of the house in the 1840s and 1850s.

In a remarkable piece of historical detective work, David discovers how the house came to be built as a merchant's residence by a canny property developer at a time when Liverpool was one of the great trading ports of the British Empire.

He then uncovers the story of the very first tenant – a customs clerk with a taste for fine furniture and the high life. David explores what happens to his lavish lifestyle when the money dries up.

The second resident, James Orr and his wife Ann, are an apparently ordinary middle-class, newly-wed couple. But they prove to be anything but as David discovers that James and Ann have spent their early lives as servants. The couple have made their way to the top of Liverpool society through hard work and a series of canny financial decisions that bring them enormous wealth.

David then discovers a darker tale when he searches for evidence of the cotton broker, Wilfred Steele. Wilfred's story leads David in extraordinary directions. He discovers a portrait of Wilfred hanging in the Walker Art Gallery. But then the evidence leads him to debtors' prison and eventually to America, where David discovers that Wilfred's attempts to escape his past have had tragic consequences for his family back home.

📺 SUBSCRIBE FOR MORE ▶️ https://www.youtube.com/@LifeThroughTimeTV

Different lives within these walls

Each episode of this fascinating, presenter-led history series tells the unique personal stories of all the people who lived in one particular house, from the time it was built until today.

Through a combination of first-hand testimony, archive film and careful detective work, we'll find out who the different residents were over time, from the first people onwards. We'll explore what their lives were like while they lived there, and how the house changed over the years. Ultimately, by following the stories of individual residents and the times in which they lived, we'll provide a distinctive social history of the UK over time and of the place they called home.

This video sheds light not only on the heartbreaking loss suffered by Colette's loved ones, but also on the breakthroughs in forensic science that brought a cold case killer to justice.

snippet.title: Island Hopping: The Strategy That Defeated Japan in the Pacific War
snippet.description:
🎥 Watch 300+ exclusive videos on Youtube► https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCMmaBzfCCwZ2KqaBJjkj0fw/join or Patreon ► https://www.patreon.com/kingsandgenerals

Kings and Generals' historical animated documentary series covering the Pacific War continues with a video on the Island hopping campaign - the strategy that defeated Japan in the Pacific War. After Midway and Guadalcanal, the United States opens a new road across the Pacific: Nimitz’s Central Pacific island-hopping campaign. This episode follows the brutal first steps through the Gilbert and Marshall Islands, where American naval power, Marines, Army troops, carriers, battleships, and amphibious vehicles collide with Japan’s fortified atolls. Operation Galvanic begins with the invasions of Makin and Tarawa, where reefs, tides, poor intelligence, and determined Japanese defenses turn the beaches into killing grounds. The lessons paid for in blood then shape Operation Flintlock, as the Americans bypass stronger positions, strike Kwajalein, seize Majuro, and overwhelm Roi-Namur. The campaign expands with Operation Hailstone, the devastating carrier raid on Truk, before the final battles for Eniwetok and Parry open the way toward the Marianas. Along the way, the video explains why the Central Pacific route mattered, how American industry changed the balance at sea, and why Japan’s island fortress strategy could not stop the advance. From Tarawa’s slaughter to Kwajalein’s breakthrough, this is the story of how the United States cracked Japan’s outer defensive perimeter and transformed island hopping into the main Allied path toward victory in the Pacific War, in one of history’s hardest amphibious learning curves ever attempted.

Kings and Generals animated documentary series on the history of Rome and Antiquity continues with a video on the Second Punic War. Hannibal Barca nearly destroyed Rome — and this is the full story of how the Second Punic War became one of the most legendary conflicts in ancient history. This video follows the rise of the Barcid family after Carthage’s humiliation in the First Punic War, from Hamilcar Barca’s campaigns in Iberia to the young Hannibal’s oath never to be a friend of Rome. As Carthage rebuilds its power in Spain, Rome is distracted by Illyrian pirates and Gallic uprisings, until the crisis at Saguntum finally ignites a war that will reshape the Mediterranean. Hannibal’s answer is one of the boldest military campaigns ever attempted: instead of waiting for Rome in Iberia or Africa, he marches north, crosses the Rhone, fights through the Alps, and invades Italy with a battered but dangerous army. What follows is a chain of Roman disasters - Ticinus, Trebia, Lake Trasimene, and finally Cannae, where Hannibal delivers one of the most studied tactical victories in history. But Rome refuses to surrender. While Hannibal struggles to turn battlefield victories into final victory, the war expands across Sicily, Spain, Macedon, southern Italy, and North Africa. Syracuse falls, Tarentum changes hands, Hasdrubal marches to Italy and dies at the Metaurus, and a new Roman commander rises: Publius Cornelius Scipio. Scipio conquers New Carthage, defeats Carthaginian armies in Iberia, invades Africa, wins over Numidian allies, and forces Hannibal’s recall. At Zama, the two greatest generals of the war finally meet in the battle that decides the fate of Carthage, Rome, and the ancient Mediterranean.

snippet.description:
Discover the secrets behind the Colosseum's enduring strength and the massive restoration project preserving this ancient Roman icon for future generations.

Join us on a fascinating journey through the history and engineering marvels of the Colosseum, the world's largest and most famous amphitheater. This video reveals how Emperor Vespasian's vision became a 2,000-year-old symbol of Rome, exploring the ingenious Roman construction techniques, the use of travertine and marble, and the complex restoration work now underway. Learn about the challenges faced by restorers as they clean centuries of grime, repair cracks, and ensure the Colosseum remains waterproof and structurally sound.

We delve into the Colosseum's turbulent past - from epic gladiator games and its transformation through earthquakes and looting, to its role as a quarry for other Roman monuments. See how public-private partnerships, like the collaboration with TODS Group, are reshaping the future of Italy’s cultural heritage. Discover how cutting-edge monitoring technology, careful conservation, and innovative fundraising are securing the Colosseum's place in modern Rome while respecting its storied past.

Whether you're passionate about Roman history, architecture, or modern restoration, this video uncovers the timeless legacy and ongoing saga of the Colosseum. Explore how preserving the world's wonders is a shared responsibility and why the fate of Rome's greatest monument matters to us all.

snippet.description:

54:39 Indigenous Communities Under Pressure
57:00 Conclusion

To his detractors, Javier Milei is rude, ignorant and a danger to democracy. He’s also undoubtedly one of the world’s most infamous politicians, and the new face of populism. We profile Argentina’s chainsaw-wielding president and meet his closest supporters.

After his first year in power, inflation is down from 25.5% to 2.4%. A tax amnesty, allowing the wealthy to repatriate money hidden abroad, has brought €30 billion back into the country’s banking system. Like most of the elite, Argentinian business man – Mariano La Torre – is delighted by Milei’s economic policy: “For economic policy, I’d give him 10 out of 10 even 11 out of 10 if I could. It’s perfect. I take my hat off to him. This is the most important change in a century.” After years living in Oslo, he’s preparing to return to Buenos Aires.   

For others, however, the effects have been brutal. “I don’t have a job, my mother is disabled and I have to pay the rent. What am I going to do?” laments Turky, one of the 50,000 civil servants who have lost their jobs. Despite the inflation, pensions have been frozen and now even those on the lowest incomes have to pay for their own medicines. 77-year-old Ruben has had to return to work.

Juan Luis González is a journalist who has been investigating the president’s messianic style for several years. “Milei sees himself as a prophet. For him, religion is the ultimate goal,” he explains. When his beloved dog, Conan, died, he had five clones created. In private messages obtained by González, the president explains how these clones inspire his policies. “One of them is Conan’s reincarnation … the clones are also his connection to God.”

The Gran Chaco forest is the second largest forest in South America after the Amazon. But it is being destroyed by bulldozers. This massive deforestation is clearing the ground for soya cultivation and cattle farming. Under Javier Milei, who denies climate change and has lifted forest protections, it is accelerating. Indigenous communities have been particularly affected. “We are losing all our resources, the things that keep us peasant families alive,” despairs Daniel. “Our culture is disappearing.”

From the vast wilderness of the north of the country, threatened by the acceleration of lithium mining, to the bourgeois neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires, this is an immersion in Javier Milei’s ultra-liberal Argentina.

snippet.description:
They left Ireland chasing a dream… but only 3 came back alive. 🔔 Subscribe and join us on this journey around the world → https://bit.ly/WorldView-Documentary

00:00 – The Addergoole 14: A Village’s Dream
02:15 – Life in Ireland in 1912
05:20 – The Journey to the Titanic
08:30 – Hopes, Superstitions & Farewells
12:00 – Life Onboard: Third-Class Reality

The story of the RMS Titanic has been told in grand style many times: the monumental, unsinkable ship, the almost unbelievable pride of its owners, and the terrible events of 1912. Waking the Titanic is something new: a living history told on a small scale, but no less poignant. Fourteen young people, aged 17 to 32, from the impoverished community of Addergoole, County Mayo, decided to emigrate. Through stylized reenactments, the docudrama recreates a joyful trip to the nearby town to buy a new hat for the voyage, because the ladies in America are well-dressed; a young couple's wedding before the voyage; the young shop girl measuring a child's finger with a piece of string so she can send him a ring from the United States; the brother reading his sister's tea leaves and warning her not to board the ship; A ticket sent from America that was spent to buy a new cow, thus saving a life, and the day fourteen eager people left the only world they knew in search of a dream. Focusing on the drama of anticipation that preceded this fateful voyage, the story of Addergoole 14 and what happened to them aboard the Titanic is told using detailed accounts passed down to family members by people of the time and interviews with descendants of the survivors. This is not simply a retelling of the Titanic's story. It is a unique account of the hope and loss suffered by the inhabitants of a small village in the west of Ireland whose sons and daughters set out in search of a better life only to be enslaved by the tragic fate of the world's largest ship. Only 3 of the 14 members of the group survived the sinking. On the other side of the Atlantic, the story is also embodied in the lives of 96 direct descendants of the survivors, whose voices form both the heart and the epilogue of this tale.

snippet.title: The Mobster Who Discovered a Better Weapon than Violence
snippet.description:
Johnny Dio wasn’t a hitman. He wasn’t a flashy boss.
And he didn’t need guns to control entire industries.

Long before “white-collar crime” became a household term, Johnny Dio discovered something far more powerful than violence: paperwork, unions, and the appearance of legitimacy.

In this video, we uncover the true story of Johnny Dio — the mob figure who helped transform organized crime from street-level brutality into institutional control. By manipulating labor laws, creating fake union locals, and selling “labor peace” to terrified business owners, Dio built a criminal empire that operated in plain sight.

This isn’t the story of a gangster who ruled with fear.
It’s the story of a man who learned how to weaponize the system itself.

In this documentary-style breakdown, you’ll learn:
-Who Johnny Dio really was and why most people have never heard of him
-How “paper locals” allowed the Mafia to control unions without violence
-Why business owners asked Dio for help instead of calling the police
-How his methods influenced modern white-collar and organized crime
-Why federal investigators struggled for decades to stop him

Johnny Dio represents the moment the Mafia learned how to wear suits, hire lawyers, and steal legally — or at least look legal while doing it.

If you’re interested in true crime, Mafia history, labor racketeering, or the hidden mechanics of organized crime, this story reveals how power really works when violence becomes optional.

📌 Watch until the end to understand why Johnny Dio’s legacy still shapes modern crime — and why his methods were more dangerous than any gun.
